title: Nikkei 225 Surges Over 2,200 Points as AI Semiconductor Rally Reignites
excerpt: Japan's benchmark index jumped more than 3% on Wednesday, led by heavyweight chip stocks, as strong U.S. tech earnings and falling oil prices revived risk appetite across Asian markets.
body:
• The Nikkei 225 surged over 2,200 points on Wednesday, climbing more than 3% as semiconductor and AI-linked stocks led a broad Asian rally.
  • Tokyo Electron and Advantest each gained over 5%, continuing a rally that has made chip-related names account for roughly 25–35% of the Nikkei's total market value.
  • The rebound follows an 8.1% slump in July and comes after the Nikkei posted its strongest quarterly gain on record — 37% — in the April–June period.
  • Falling oil prices, U.S.–Iran diplomacy on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and Wall Street's record highs fueled the broader risk-on mood.

Chip Stocks Power Japan's Sharpest Rally in Weeks

Japan's Nikkei 225 surged more than 2,200 points on Wednesday, reclaiming ground lost during a punishing July selloff as investors piled back into semiconductor and artificial intelligence-linked stocks.

The benchmark index climbed roughly 3.0% to trade above 65,400, according to Reuters, with Tokyo Electron and Advantest — the two heaviest chip contributors to the index — each advancing more than 5%. The broader Topix also gained, though less dramatically, as the rally remained concentrated in technology names.

The session marked one of the Nikkei's strongest single-day gains since early May, when the index first broke through 63,000 on optimism over strong U.S. tech earnings and signs of a U.S.–Iran peace framework.

Reclaiming July's Losses

The rally arrives after a bruising stretch for Japan's equity market. The Nikkei slumped 8.1% in July, according to Barron's, as a sharp pullback in global chip stocks dragged down Tokyo's semiconductor-heavy benchmark. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 18.5% from its late-June peak, while South Korea's Kospi dropped more than 22%.

That correction interrupted what had been a historic run. The Nikkei recorded a 37% gain in the April–June quarter, its sharpest quarterly advance in data going back to 1965, according to Reuters. The index closed June at 70,062.

Wednesday's rebound suggests the correction may have run its course. "Investor money is concentrated on high-flying chip-related shares. There is no need to buy value shares when technology shares are giving solid returns," Kazuaki Shimada, chief strategist at IwaiCosmo Securities, told Reuters.

"This is just the beginning of their rally. Investors will continue to hunt stocks that are related to AI data centres."

— Kazuaki Shimada, Chief Strategist, IwaiCosmo Securities

Three Waves of the AI Trade

The AI-driven rally in Japanese equities has unfolded in distinct phases. The first wave lifted familiar names — SoftBank Group, Advantest, and Tokyo Electron. A second leg drew in suppliers such as fibre-optic cable makers Fujikura and Furukawa Electric.

Now a third wave is spreading into components and power infrastructure essential to data centre operations. Murata Manufacturing and Taiyo Yuden, leading producers of multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) used to regulate power in AI servers, have emerged as fresh engines of the advance. Murata shares have climbed 268% this year, while Taiyo Yuden has surged 438%, according to Reuters.

Memory maker Kioxia, which overtook Toyota Motor in market capitalisation, trails only Taiyo Yuden in year-to-date Nikkei gains. Ibiden, a supplier to Nvidia, is up 292%. Chip-related names now account for about 25% of the Nikkei's total value, a weighting that rises to roughly 35% when component makers like Murata, Sony Group, and Kyocera are included, according to Takamasa Ikeda, senior portfolio manager at GCI Asset Management.

Global Tailwinds

The Tokyo rally did not happen in isolation. Wall Street's S&P 500 and Nasdaq both hit all-time highs on Tuesday, powered by strong hyperscaler earnings that reinforced the AI capital expenditure thesis. Google's cloud revenue growth accelerated to 82%, Microsoft's to 43%, and Amazon's to 37%, with backlogs rising $300 billion and capex guidance increasing $150 billion, according to Société Générale.

Falling oil prices added to the risk-on mood. Brent crude dropped 1.4% to $78.27 a barrel — far below its July peak of $102 — after Qatar said mediators were making progress on a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington could reach a deal with Iran "today or tomorrow."

The yen held near 157.43 per dollar, steadying after Japan and the United States conducted a rare joint yen-buying intervention last week. Lower oil prices eased inflation concerns, pushing 10-year U.S. Treasury yields down to 4.603% from last week's 4.747% peak.

What Indian Investors Should Watch

The Nikkei's AI-driven surge carries implications for Indian markets and investors. The concentration of gains in semiconductor supply chains underscores how deeply Japan is embedded in the global AI infrastructure buildout — a theme India's own semiconductor ambitions aim to tap through partnerships with Japanese firms including Tokyo Electron and Renesas Electronics.

Indian mutual funds offering Japan-focused ETFs have seen increased inflows this year, and the Nikkei's outperformance of both U.S. and European benchmarks has drawn attention from wealth managers serving the Indian diaspora. The risk, as GCI's Ikeda warned, is concentration: if the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index corrects further, "the same fate will be inevitable for the Nikkei."

What's Next

All eyes now turn to the Bank of Japan's next policy signals. U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent said he was confident BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda would "do what is best" for the economy — language markets interpreted as encouragement for further rate increases. A stronger yen, while negative for exporters, could also moderate inflation and support domestic consumer stocks that have lagged the AI rally.

For now, Japan's semiconductor trade shows no sign of cooling. With hyperscaler spending accelerating and AI infrastructure demand broadening into new component categories, Tokyo's chip stocks remain the market's center of gravity.
